lead: This entry covers two separate practices that looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities group together: prolonged food fasting (going beyond 24 hours without eating, typically 5 to 20 days) and 'dopamine fasting', in which a person abstains from stimulating behaviours such as phone use, gaming or pornography [1][2]. People use extended fasts to lose body fat quickly, since lower body fat is widely said to reveal jawline, cheekbones and neck definition. People use dopamine fasting to build self-control and free up time and focus for gym, sleep and skincare habits [2][4].

Dopamine fasting was developed as a cognitive behavioural approach by California psychologist Cameron Sepah and attracted media coverage from October 2019 [2]. Sepah has said the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviours rather than literally lower dopamine, and that the name is a catchy label; several neuroscientists have criticised the idea that the brain can be 'reset' this way [2][4].

Fasting research covers ketosis, weight loss and cardiometabolic markers, and clinicians document risks of prolonged fasts, including electrolyte loss, gallstones and refeeding syndrome [1][5]. Neither practice has been studied for facial appearance.

angle.text: Extended fasting is used for rapid fat loss, which people say sharpens facial definition. Dopamine fasting is used to cut time-consuming impulsive habits, in the hope of more consistent training, sleep and skincare.

paras: The practice was developed by Cameron Sepah as a form of cognitive behavioural therapy and is associated in media reports with Silicon Valley [2]. In Harvard Health's account, he framed it as a way to loosen the pull of constant digital cues such as notifications, tolerate boredom and enjoy simpler activities, and linked it to six behaviours: emotional eating, excessive internet and gaming, gambling and shopping, pornography and masturbation, novelty seeking and recreational drugs [4].

Versions vary in strictness. Some limit only online technology, while others also drop work, exercise, physical contact and conversation, and an extreme version would be full sensory deprivation [2]. The moderate schedule described by Sepah, as reported by Grinspoon, is one to four screen-free hours at the end of the day, one weekend day outdoors, a weekend each quarter and a week each year [4]. People in appearance communities adopt it to cut hours lost to scrolling and redirect them to training, sleep and routines.

Vice (Katie Way, 17 October 2019) described it as a wellness trend akin to Silicon Valley biohacking, and the New York Times (Nellie Bowles, 7 November 2019) reported a practitioner finding everyday life more exciting [2]. Psych Central (13 November 2019), Mic (30 December 2019) and Marie Claire (10 January 2020) followed, and Inc. covered a Harvard doctor's view on detoxes in June 2024 [2].

Harvard psychiatrist Peter Grinspoon called Sepah's approach sensible but not new, and criticised ever more extreme, ascetic versions (Harvard Health Blog, 26 February 2020) [2][4]. He wrote that avoiding stimulation does not lower dopamine and that treating dopamine like a drug to be 'tolerance-broken' misreads the science [4].

University of Reading neuroscientist Ciara McCabe disputed the idea that avoiding a stimulus resets the brain and argued that removing a stimulus reduces dopamine stimulation, not dopamine itself; UConn's John Salamone described the practice as nebulously defined [2]. Sepah told the New York Times that dopamine is a mechanism explaining how addictions get reinforced and makes a catchy title [4].

A 2022 paper in Lifestyle Medicine examined dopamine fasting as a possible intervention for behavioural addiction, and a December 2024 genetically informed study of adults aged 30 to 45 in Computers in Human Behavior found higher screen time associated with higher impulsivity [2].

Fasting is abstaining from food and sometimes drink. Wikipedia distinguishes intermittent fasting, alternate-day fasting (a day under about a quarter of usual energy alternating with normal eating), and prolonged, extended or water fasting beyond 24 hours, typically 5 to 20 days; variants include juice and dry fasting [1].

In prolonged fasting, early gluconeogenesis gives way to ketosis, with ketones becoming the brain's main fuel. Sodium, potassium and magnesium fall, which can cause hyponatremia. Average weight loss is about 0.9 kg per day in week one and about 0.3 kg per day by week three, and in the early phase roughly two-thirds of the weight lost is lean tissue, shifting later to a fat-to-lean ratio of roughly 7:6 [1].

In looksmaxxing discussion, multi-day fasts are used for quick drops in body fat before photos or events, with the aim of sharper jaw and cheek definition. Online accounts range from water fasts to fasts planned with AI chatbot help, such as a 2026 Hacker News post describing fat loss experiments with ChatGPT and water fasting [3].

A 2021 review found moderate alternate-day fasting for two to six months reduced body weight, BMI and cardiometabolic risk factors in overweight or obese adults, comparable to calorie restriction. Wikipedia reports weaker evidence that intermittent fasting under 24 hours produces sustained weight loss in obese adults, and states there is no sound clinical evidence that fasting extends human lifespan [1].

Angus Barbieri, a Scot, fasted for 382 days from 14 June 1965 to 30 June 1966 under medical monitoring, living on tea, coffee, sparkling water, vitamins and yeast extract, and lost about 125 kg [1]. Fasting is also a feature of Ramadan, Yom Kippur, Lent and ascetic traditions in Hinduism and Buddhism, and was used as political protest by Gandhi [1].

Refeeding syndrome follows reintroduction of food after starvation, when insulin-driven synthesis consumes phosphate, magnesium and potassium that are already depleted; it can cause cardiac, neurologic and other complications and can be fatal, with abnormal heart rhythms the most common cause of death [5]. It usually appears within about four days of refeeding and can follow roughly four to five days without food [1][5]. Fasting, especially with rapid weight loss, can also raise gallstone risk [1]. Wikipedia describes fasting for 'detoxification' as having little scientific basis [1].

No studies found testing either practice for facial appearance. Research exists on alternate-day and intermittent fasting for weight and cardiometabolic markers, and a 2022 paper discussed dopamine fasting as a possible behavioural-addiction intervention [1][2].

lore.intro: Fasting for fat loss and discipline-focused 'detoxes' circulate in self-improvement communities, including on Hacker News [3].

claims.claim: Dopamine fasting resets the brain's reward system
claims.believers: Proponents say abstaining from stimulation restores motivation and self-control [2].
claims.experts: Sepah says the goal is reducing impulsive behaviour, not lowering dopamine; McCabe and Grinspoon dispute a brain 'reset' [2][4].

claims.claim: Multi-day fasts quickly reveal a sharper face by burning fat
claims.believers: People fasting for fat loss describe rapid weight reductions [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports about two-thirds of early weight loss in prolonged fasts is lean tissue, and documents refeeding syndrome risk [1].

claims.claim: A short digital break builds discipline for gym and sleep
claims.believers: Advocates describe one to four screen-free hours or a day outdoors as freeing time for training and routines [4].
claims.experts: Grinspoon calls this sensible but not new, similar to mindfulness and sleep hygiene [4].

claims.claim: Extreme versions that avoid exercise, music, food and people are better
claims.believers: Some online versions extend the fast to nearly all stimulation [2].
claims.experts: Grinspoon calls these extreme versions unhealthy and says human interaction was never part of Sepah's idea [4].

claims.claim: Fasting for several days is a detox
claims.believers: Alternative-medicine promoters say fasting cleanses the body [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes detoxification claims as having little scientific basis and notes deaths among patients of Linda Hazzard's regimens [1].

claims.claim: Water fasts are safe if you stay hydrated
claims.believers: Participants point to long supervised fasts such as Barbieri's [1][3].
claims.experts: Barbieri's was medically monitored; clinicians describe electrolyte loss and refeeding syndrome, which can be fatal [1][5].

name: Extended fasting / dopamine fasts

card.summary: Abstaining from food or stimulation to 'reset'; the behavioural version is loosely defined and extended fasting carries real medical risks.
card.note: Refeeding syndrome after prolonged fasting can be fatal.

quick.overview:
Two practices share this entry: multi-day food fasting, and dopamine fasting, where people avoid stimulating habits such as phones or gaming.

No studies were found on appearance outcomes, and experts quoted in coverage dispute the 'reset' framing of dopamine fasting.
quick.mechanism: Extended fasting shifts the body into ketosis. Dopamine fasting is described by its originator as reducing impulsive behaviour, not lowering dopamine itself.
quick.risks: Prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte loss, gallstones, lean-mass loss and refeeding syndrome, which can be fatal. Dopamine fasting has no specific physical harms reported, though critics call its premise unscientific.
